before.rationale: John Stuart Mill, 1848–1873: the question asks whether Whether people develop cooperative habits depends more on their social surroundings than on inherited tendencies. Research checked: The Subjection of Women calls present female character an artificial product of repression and social training. The exact condition requiring evidence is cooperative habits’ social versus inherited predominance. Broad principles cannot establish this mechanism without an explicit supported bridge. Natural capacities may differ; the text does not measure IQ heritability or infer every specific trait from its argument about imposed gender roles. No sufficiently specific position was located in those checked passages. This is missing evidence, not a balanced or neutral position.

after.rationale: Utilitarianism, Chapter III, paragraphs beginning “This firm foundation” and “They are also familiar”, explains how cooperation identifies a person’s aims with those of others; stronger social ties, education and institutions develop this into habitual practical regard for others. This provides a specific mechanism for socially acquired cooperative habits, beyond merely advocating cooperation. Qualified agreement: Mill also recognises a natural social feeling, so this is an inference about the development of habits, not denial of innate capacities or an empirical heritability estimate.

before.rationale: John Stuart Mill, 1848–1873: the question asks whether People’s immediate reactions to what they consider right or wrong are shaped more by biological predispositions than by upbringing and culture. Research checked: The Subjection of Women calls present female character an artificial product of repression and social training. The exact condition requiring evidence is immediate moral reactions’ biological versus learned predominance. Broad principles cannot establish this mechanism without an explicit supported bridge. Natural capacities may differ; the text does not measure IQ heritability or infer every specific trait from its argument about imposed gender roles. No sufficiently specific position was located in those checked passages. This is missing evidence, not a balanced or neutral position.

after.rationale: Utilitarianism, Chapter III, paragraphs beginning “On the other hand” and “Unhappily it is also susceptible”, states Mill’s own belief that moral feelings are acquired and explains how early impressions, education and sanctions can attach the authority of conscience to very different objects. The paragraph beginning “This feeling, when disinterested” locates the felt reaction in associations from childhood and past experience. These passages specifically bridge acquired moral feelings to reactions of conscience. Qualified disagreement rather than a blanket rejection of biology: Chapter V also recognises natural retaliation and sympathy as components of the sentiment of justice.

before.rationale: The Subjection of Women describes observed female character as artificially formed by repression and selective social cultivation. Development through habit and opportunity in On Liberty and the Subjection supports learned self-control rather than an inherited racial destiny, without a specific trait estimate.

It does not provide a racial comparison or a quantified causal estimate.
